Oral Disease Recognition

Learning Objectives:

1.Recognize the early and advanced signs of early childhood caries (ECC) and describe its risk factors in the context of pediatric feeding.
2.Identify dental erosion and differentiate intrinsic (GERD, rumination) from extrinsic (dietary acid) etiologies by clinical pattern.
3.Distinguish caries from erosion based on appearance, distribution, and associated history and understand why this distinction changes the clinical response.
4.Recognize common oral mucosal conditions relevant to feeding: candidiasis, aphthous ulcers, herpetic stomatitis, and mucositis.
5.Apply a structured oral screening approach during feeding assessments and identify findings that warrant urgent vs. routine dental referral.

Section 1: Early Childhood Caries (ECC)

Early childhood caries (ECC) is defined by the American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry as the presence of at least one decayed, missing due to decay, or filled tooth surface in any primary tooth of a child 71 months of age or younger. It remains the most prevalent chronic pediatric disease in the United States, affecting approximately 23% of children between the ages of two and five. ECC develops from a combination of genetic and environmental factors, specifically the interaction between cariogenic bacteria, primarily Streptococcus mutans, fermentable carbohydrates, and host susceptibility factors such as enamel integrity and salivary function. Among the strongest predictors of future caries is a child's previous caries experience.

From a modifiable standpoint, sugar intake is the most critical risk factor, particularly when sugars are consumed frequently or in forms that linger in the mouth for extended periods, such as juice in sippy cups, sticky snacks, or sugared medications. Research has shown that children with S-ECC exhibit notably reduced chewing performance compared to caries-free controls, with scores falling in a range similar to those seen in children with eosinophilic esophagitis and abnormal swallowing. Children experiencing severe ECC may begin to favor softer, sweeter foods as a way of managing pain, inadvertently creating a cycle that accelerates caries progression. As avoidance of harder textures increases, so does reliance on cariogenic foods, which in turn drives further decay.

Stages of Early Childhood Caries

Understanding how caries progresses can help feeding team members recognize when a dental referral is warranted and how urgently one is needed.

Stage 1: White Spot Lesion

The earliest visible sign of caries appears as chalky white or opaque areas on smooth tooth surfaces. At this stage, the enamel is demineralized but still intact, making this the only stage that is fully reversible. With timely fluoride intervention and dietary changes, the tooth can remineralize without the need for restorative treatment.

Photo Credit: Tim Wright DDS, 

Stage 2: Early Cavitation

As caries progresses, white or yellow-brown discoloration may appear alongside surface roughness or early breakdown. Once surface integrity is compromised, remineralization alone is no longer sufficient and dental restoration is needed.

Photo Credit: Tim Wright DDS, 

Stage 3: Established Caries

At this stage, cavitation is visible and ranges from brown to black in color, with clear involvement of the underlying dentin. Children may experience pain when eating hot, cold, or sweet foods. A dental referral at this stage is urgent.

Photo Credit: Tim Wright DDS, 

Stage 4: Abscess / Non-Vital Tooth

In the most advanced stage, the affected tooth may appear gray or black. Swelling, a fistula, or abscess may be present, and the child may show no fever despite harboring a chronic infection. This stage requires urgent or emergent dental care.

Figure X. Parulis associated with a dental abscess. Image by Damdent, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

Integrating Caries Risk Assessment into Feeding Evaluations

Caries risk assessment can be incorporated naturally into routine feeding evaluations. When gathering history or observing feeding, team members can screen for the following indicators:

Key Screening Indicators

  • • Continued bottle or sippy cup use with fluids other than water
  • • Sleeping with a bottle
  • • Frequent between-meal sugary snacks or drinks
  • • Visible plaque or white spot lesions on the teeth
  • • A history of previous caries experience in the child or their caregivers

Clinical Recommendations

Feeding recommendations and caries prevention share considerable common ground. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends:

  • • Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, with continued breastfeeding alongside complementary foods for one year or longer
  • • Weaning from the bottle by 12 months of age
  • • Limiting juice to no more than four ounces per day for children ages one to three, and avoiding juice entirely before age one
  • • Encouraging water between meals, with fluoridated water preferred
  • • Reducing the frequency of added sugar in foods and drinks
  • • Wiping the gums or erupting teeth after nighttime breastfeeding

Because these recommendations align closely with broader feeding goals, the feeding team is well positioned to reinforce them as part of a coordinated, family-centered approach to care.

Section 2: Dental Erosion

Unlike dental caries, which results from bacterial acid production, dental erosion involves the chemical dissolution of enamel and dentin by acids from external or systemic sources rather than oral bacteria. This is of particular relevance in young children, as primary teeth are more vulnerable to erosion than permanent teeth due to their thinner enamel, lower mineral content, and greater acid solubility.

Clinical Considerations and Management of Dental Erosion

Once dental erosion is identified, its location and severity should be documented using a standardized scoring scale such as the BEWE or Keels-Coffield scale. Noting the pattern of erosion can also provide valuable clues about its underlying cause.

                                                                                                 Source: Martha Ann Keels, DDS, PhD and Kristina D. Coffield, DDS (2002)

Etiology and Referral

In pediatric patients, the location of erosion can offer important diagnostic insight. Erosion on the lingual surfaces of the upper incisors is more commonly associated with GERD, while erosion driven by dietary acids can appear on any tooth surface depending on how the child consumes acidic foods or beverages. When GERD is suspected, referral to the child's medical provider is warranted. Similarly, if bulimia is suspected, referral to an appropriate medical provider should be initiated promptly.

Dietary Counseling

When dietary acids are identified as the primary contributor, caregivers should be counseled to reduce acidic food and beverage exposure. Avoiding swishing acidic drinks across tooth surfaces is a simple but important behavioral modification that can meaningfully slow erosion progression.

Fluoride and Restorative Management

Children with erosive tooth wear benefit from an additional fluoride source, such as a stannous fluoride-containing toothpaste or rinse, to help protect remaining tooth structure. Restorative intervention should be delayed as long as possible to allow for ongoing monitoring, and when treatment does become necessary, minimally invasive techniques are preferred to preserve as much natural tooth structure as possible.

Section 3: Oral Mucosal Conditions Relevant to Eating

Beyond the teeth themselves, the oral mucosa can present with a range of conditions that are directly relevant to feeding function and comfort. Mucosal changes may affect a child's ability to latch, tolerate texture, manage a bolus, or sustain adequate oral intake. Because feeding team members routinely observe the oral cavity as part of their evaluations, familiarity with common mucosal conditions can support earlier identification, appropriate referral, and coordinated care with pediatric dental colleagues.

A scoping review of 20 clinical studies involving nearly 86,000 children identified the most frequently occurring oral mucosal conditions in pediatric populations. Aphthous ulcerations were the most common, affecting approximately 1.82% of children, followed by trauma-associated lesions and herpes simplex virus (HSV)-associated lesions, each present in approximately 1.33% of cases. Geographic tongue and fissured tongue were also among the most commonly observed findings.

Xerostomia (Dry Mouth)

While more commonly associated with adults, xerostomia is highly relevant to pediatric feeding teams. Reduced salivary flow significantly impacts bolus formation and swallowing safety.

Clinical Contexts & Etiologies

Medications

Over 500 medications known to cause hyposalivation.

Post-Radiation

Direct damage to salivary gland acinar cells.

GVHD

Graft-versus-host disease affecting mucosal integrity.

Ectodermal Dysplasia

Congenital absence or reduction of gland function.

lightbulb Clinical Insight

Beyond its impact on comfort and feeding function, reduced salivary flow can also increase a child's risk for dental caries and oral candidiasis, making early identification and dental coordination particularly important in these populations.
